story: David Guetta, born and raised in Paris, began as a DJ in Parisian nightclubs and discovered house music on French radio in 1987. Axwell, Steve Angello and Sebastian Ingrosso formed Swedish House Mafia in late 2008 and, with Avicii, took progressive house into the mainstream. From 2009 Guetta scored crossover hits with pop and hip-hop singers: Kelly Rowland on "When Love Takes Over", the Black Eyed Peas on "I Gotta Feeling", Sia on "Titanium". Tim Bergling, born in Stockholm in 1989, taught himself on a pirated copy of FL Studio, and as Avicii had his first Billboard Hot 100 entry with "Levels" in 2011. In the late 2000s the American music industry took up the term EDM to re-brand US rave culture. Mixmag called the result a "drop-heavy, stadium-filling" main stage sound. Avicii and Swedish House Mafia played arenas rather than clubs; in December 2011 Swedish House Mafia became the first electronic act to sell out Madison Square Garden. Avicii's 2013 "Wake Me Up", sung by soul singer Aloe Blacc, drew on bluegrass. The American EDM market began to wane in 2016, and in April that year Guetta and Showtek released a single called "The Death of EDM".

disagreements: Window: our record says 2011-2015; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electronic_dance_music?action=raw places Guetta's crossover hits from 2009 ("In 2009, [[French house]] musician [[David Guetta]] began to regularly achieve [[Crossover music|crossover hits]]") and the end at 2016 ("the American popular EDM market started to wane in 2016"). The record's window is the peak, not the start and end.

Origin: our record says Paris and Stockholm; the people are from there (Guetta, Paris; Avicii, Stockholm; Swedish House Mafia, Swedish), but the EDM article tells the pop crossover as a US market story ("the American music industry's adoption of the term EDM in the late 2000s was an attempt to re-brand US \"rave culture\"").
notes: No home-language article applies; the genre has no Wikipedia article of its own under 'EDM-pop', so the story is built from the Electronic dance music article (US popularity section) and the artists' articles. Our markers (supersaws, big-room kicks) are not described for the pop songs in the pages read; only Mixmag's 'drop-heavy, stadium-filling' description and the later 'big room' sound appear. Dropped for length: Billboard's Dance/Electronic Songs chart (January 2013), sourced in the EDM article.
